whyItExists.problem: Many programming tasks require repeating an operation — process every item in a list, sum 100 numbers, retry a request 3 times. Writing each step manually is impossible for large datasets.
whyItExists.solution: Loops repeat a block of code multiple times. JavaScript has for (fixed count), while (condition-based), for...of (iterable items), and for...in (object keys).
whyItExists.whenToUse: When processing every item in an array, repeating an action a set number of times, or continuing until a condition is met.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For arrays, prefer higher-order methods (map, filter, forEach, reduce) — they are more expressive and less error-prone. Use classic loops for index-level control or complex iteration.

explainModes.beginner: A loop is like pressing 'repeat' on a music player. 'Play this 10 times' is a for loop. 'Keep playing until the battery dies' is a while loop. 'Play each song in this playlist' is a for...of loop.
explainModes.simple: for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) runs 5 times. while (condition) runs until the condition is false. for (const item of array) goes through each array item. break exits the loop early; continue skips to the next iteration.
explainModes.standard: The for loop has three parts: initialiser, condition, and update. for...of iterates over any iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets) and is preferred over indexed for loops for simple iteration. for...in iterates over object keys — use it carefully as it includes inherited properties.
explainModes.technical: Loops interact with the call stack directly. An infinite loop (while (true) with no break) blocks the JS thread and freezes the browser. Async iteration (for await...of) iterates asynchronous iterables — useful for processing streams. Array methods like forEach, map, and filter are implemented as loops internally but express intent more clearly.
explainModes.deepDive: JavaScript engines optimise hot loops with JIT compilation — tight loops with consistent types are compiled to machine code. Loop unrolling and SIMD vectorisation can happen automatically. Avoid modifying an array while iterating over it (splice inside forEach) — iterate a copy or use filter to create a new array. Generator functions (function*) produce custom iterables consumed by for...of.

content.text: For arrays, prefer array.find() over a for loop with break: const found = users.find(u => u.id === 2) — it's shorter and expresses intent clearly.

questions.question: Which loop is best for iterating over each item in an array when you don't need the index?
questions.explanation: for...of iterates cleanly over array items without needing an index variable. It works on any iterable: arrays, strings, Maps, Sets.

questions.question: What does the continue statement do inside a loop?
options: Restarts the loop from the beginning
Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next
questions.explanation: continue skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves to the next loop cycle. break exits the loop entirely.

faq.q: What is the difference between for...of and for...in?
faq.a: for...of iterates over iterable values (array items, string characters). for...in iterates over enumerable property KEYS of an object (including inherited ones). Use for...of for arrays; use Object.keys/values/entries for objects.

faq.q: Can I use break inside a forEach loop?
faq.a: No. break and continue only work in classic for, while, and for...of loops. forEach does not support breaking early. If you need early exit, use for...of, a classic for loop, or array.find() / array.some().
